conventions: kĕ's compound renderings are each read as one rendering of the single preposition under rule 30 and headed on the first word: *like unto* (10.1, 10.3), *according to* (10.4), *as at* (10.10, 10.15). The second English word is neither split off onto the following article or noun nor marked added, because dropping it leaves no morpheme short of a rendering of its own. A bare *as* (10.22) is the same preposition where the ASV happened to write one word.

kaʾăšer is one noncompositional unit headed on the governing preposition whether the ASV writes *as* (10.5) or the two-word *according as* (10.9); the two-word rendering is not split onto kĕ and ʾăšer.

Determiner counts in demonstrative phrases: where a demonstrative pronoun (hîʾ, zeh, ʾēlleh) stands in the phrase, it takes the one determiner the ASV writes and every article in the phrase — the noun's own and the agreement article alike — is unrepresented (10.1, 10.8, 10.10, 10.15, 10.21). Where no demonstrative morpheme stands, the article itself takes the written *this*: haYYôm → *this day* (10.13). The chapter writes both shapes, so read the phrase rather than the English.

Possessive and belonging clauses take three shapes here, decided by which morpheme is present. hāyāh present takes *hath* itself and its lĕ goes unrepresented (10.9). A verbless belonging clause gives *unto ... belongeth* whole to the lĕ heading the predicate, headed on *unto* and discontinuous around the subject (10.14). And where the clause's only preposition is a locative bĕ that has already taken its own *in*, the supplied *having* answers to no morpheme and is added, the waw the ASV leaves unrendered going unrepresented beside it (10.3).

*nor* rests on the waw alone at 10.9, where the clause's single lōʾ is spent on the determiner *no* of *no portion*, and on the fused waw+lōʾ at 10.17, where a second negative is written. Both are correct; the difference is what the Hebrew writes, and neither should be levelled to the other.
report: Checked all 48 candidate lemma groups and then read the dump end to end, since the candidate table is blind to `added` units. No construction is analysed two ways without something in the source or in the ASV licensing the difference.

הוּא Pp3ms (10.9 unrepresented vs 10.21 *He*): licensed. 10.9 writes an explicit subject noun that takes the English subject, so the resumptive pronoun is the unrendered occurrence (rule 22); both verses give the supplied copula to the written predicate (rule 20).

לְ + divine name (10.9 unrepresented vs 10.14 *unto belongeth*): licensed. 10.9 has הָיָה present, which takes *hath* and silences its preposition (rule 43); 10.14 is verbless, so the belonging verb joins the לְ heading the predicate (rule 49).

*nor* is treated two ways and both are right: the waw alone at 10.9, where the clause's single לֹא is already spent on the determiner *no*, and the fused waw+לֹא at 10.17, where a second negative is written. Rule 35's 'align what is actually there' — do not level these to each other.
כְּ compounds are consistent: *like unto* (10.1, 10.3), *according to* (10.4), *as at* (10.10, 10.15) and bare *as* (10.22) are one rendering each, fused under rule 30 and headed on the first word.

Article counts are consistent chapter-wide: each written *the* is matched to the word it stands before (10.4, 10.8, 10.14, 10.17, 10.22), agreement articles go unrepresented (10.2, 10.4, 10.10, 10.17), a demonstrative pronoun in the phrase takes the one determiner written (10.1, 10.8, 10.10, 10.15, 10.21), and the article takes *this* itself only where no demonstrative morpheme stands (10.13).

Added-blind check: the two `added` units are *having* (10.3) and *thy* (10.11), and neither has a counterpart folded into a licensing morpheme elsewhere. Supplied determiners go to their nouns, supplied copulas to their predicates, a supplied possessive goes to a present suffix (10.16, 10.21), and the only other supplied verb — *belongeth* (10.14) — has a predicate לְ to carry it, while 10.3's בְּ has already spent its word on *in* (rule 43's count sentence).

BSB 466/498 (93.6%). The Td × 19 and R × 6 classes are the documented convention difference. The singletons — 10.3 וּ, 10.7 ה, 10.9 הוּא, 10.10 בַּ, 10.13 אֶת, 10.15 אוֹתָ, 10.16 כֶם — are correct ASV-specific calls under rules 40, 32, 22 and 16. None is a genuine error, and nothing was changed to move the rate.

No promotions or amendments. The chapter's hard calls are already decided by rules 30, 32, 41, 43 and 47. The one novel call — *even* given to an appositional בְּ at 10.15 — rests on a single occurrence with no corpus row behind it and its unit note names the competing reading; a rule built on that would be paid for by every later chapter.
